literature.headline_zh: SARS-CoV-2本期文献呈现多方向研究进展
literature.lead_zh: 本期SARS-CoV-2研究集中呈现以下进展。
key_findings_zh: 总体严重急性呼吸综合征冠状病毒2阳性率为11.8%。在测序样本中,92例(13.8%)与其他呼吸道病毒共检出,包括流感病毒。最常见的谱系为XBB*(25.0%)、BA.4/BA.5*(22.1%)、JN.1*及其后代(13.6%)、BA.2*(12.6%)和BA.1*(9.0%)。Delta占基因组的8.7%,其余9.1%属于其他谱系,包括Omicron前变异株和非XBB重组株。 [10.1186/s12985-026-03262-7]
旅行者和社区病例数据中严重急性呼吸综合征冠状病毒2阳性率经常表现出一致性(66.7%的时间间隔具有显著相关性,定义为P < .05)。 [10.1177/00333549261477721]
来自32个欧洲国家的37个实验室参与了此次研究。23个实验室(62%)正确识别了严重急性呼吸综合征冠状病毒2,而20个实验室(54%)正确确定了RSV群。13个实验室成功生成了严重急性呼吸综合征冠状病毒2序列,仅有两个实验室获得了RSV序列。 [10.1128/jcm.00258-26]
我们估计,接种加强剂后,严重疾病相对风险每月增加9% [95%CI 7.4-10.5],这可能由于抗体减弱;并且每过一个历书月,相对风险还会额外增加2.4% [95%CI 1.2-3.6],这可能由于抗原漂移。 [10.64898/2026.09.14.26363077]

在484名受试者中,有432名提供了足够的随访信息用于最终分析。在432名受试者中,有210名(49%)发生了严重急性呼吸综合征冠状病毒2感染,其中182名(87%)出现了症状。在抗刺突蛋白IgG水平或抗RBD IgG水平的第10百分位至第90百分位之间,感染概率未见变化。预测概率在针对祖先严重急性呼吸综合征冠状病毒2的伪中和能力方面下降了3%,在活病毒微中和滴度方面下降了5%。在家庭接触后早期,发生感染的受试者对严重急性呼吸综合征冠状病毒2膜蛋白刺激的Th17 CD4 + T细胞激活反应增强。 [10.1016/j.lanmic.2026.101500]

literature.headline_en: Recent Severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 literature
literature.lead_en: This reporting window highlights the following research developments.
key_findings_en: Overall COVID-19 mortality rates increased from 22.3 to 27.5 per 100,000 person-months during the vaccine availability period, driven by the Delta variant surge. [10.1371/journal.pone.0358543]

The overall SARS-CoV-2 positivity rate was 11.8%. Among the sequenced samples, 92 (13.8%) showed co-detection with other respiratory viruses, including influenza. The most prevalent lineages were XBB* (25.0%), BA.4/BA.5* (22.1%), JN.1* and descendants (13.6%), BA.2* (12.6%), and BA.1* (9.0%). [10.1186/s12985-026-03262-7]
SARS-CoV-2 positivity in travelers and community case data frequently demonstrated concordance (66.7% of time intervals were significantly correlated, defined as P < .05). [10.1177/00333549261477721]

Thirty-seven laboratories from 32 European countries participated. SARS-CoV-2 was correctly identified by 23 laboratories (62%), while RSV groups were correctly determined by 20 laboratories (54%). Thirteen laboratories successfully generated SARS-CoV-2 sequences, and only two obtained RSV sequences. [10.1128/jcm.00258-26]

The review concludes that ACE2 dysregulation and lipid metabolism alterations are interconnected and play a significant role in the pathophysiology of severe COVID-19 and Long COVID. [10.1016/j.mam.2026.101519]

papers.title: Genomic surveillance of SARS-CoV-2 in Tunisia during the omicron era: insights from the national influenza & other respiratory viruses laboratory
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Omicron sublineages have dominated global SARS-CoV-2 circulation since late 2021, but there aren't enough multi-year datasets that detail lineage dynamics and genomic surveillance performance in North Africa. The National Influenza and Other Respiratory Viruses Laboratory in Tunisia has been conducting integrated SARS-CoV-2 genomic surveillance for four years. METHODS: Between 1 November 2021 and 30 September 2025, 8,635 nasopharyngeal swabs (NPS) received through the national sentinel network were tested for SARS-CoV-2 by real-time RT-PCR, of which 1,020 (11.8%) were positive. A total of 669 (65.6%) positive samples were successfully sequenced using Illumina RNA Prep with Enrichment and a respiratory virus panel. Pango lineages and GISAID clades were assigned with standard tools, and sequencing coverage, geographic representativeness, turnaround times, temporal trends, lineage diversity, mutational profiles, and phylogenetic placement were summarized descriptively. RESULTS: The overall SARS-CoV-2 positivity rate was 11.8%. Median governorate-level sequencing coverage among RT-PCR-positive samples was 60.0% (IQR 28.6-88.9), and the share of sequences closely matched the share of positives (r = 0.992), indicating near-proportional sampling.While SARS-CoV-2-positive NPS displayed several waves, including substantial peaks in mid-2022 and mid-2023 and subsequent winter peaks, each linked to the establishment or replacement of dominant Omicron lineages, testing volumes indicated recurrent winter rises. Among the 669 sequenced SARS-CoV-2-positive samples, 92 (13.8%) showed co-detection with at least one other respiratory virus, including 16 (2.4%) involving influenza viruses.XBB* lineages accounted for 25.0% of genomes, followed by BA.4/BA.5* (22.1%), JN.1* and descendants (13.6%), BA.2* (12.6%), and BA.1* (9.0%), while Delta represented 8.7% of genomes; the remaining 9.1% belonged to other lineages, including pre-Omicron variants and non-XBB recombinants. Almost all genomes belonged to Omicron-associated GISAID clades GK and GRA. Overall, sequencing quality was high (mapped reads typically ≥0.9), while Tunisian SARS-CoV-2 genomes showed a progressive increase in amino acid changes-from ~30-50 substitutions in early Delta/BA.1/BA.2 to >70-80 in later XBB and JN.1* sublineages, with some recombinants approaching 100 substitutions. Phylogenetic analyses showed that Tunisian genomes clustered within globally circulating Delta and Omicron clades. papers.title_zh: 突尼斯在奥密克戎时期严重急性呼吸综合征冠状病毒2的流行情况:来自国家流感及其他呼吸道病毒实验室的见解
papers.source_body_en: BACKGROUND: Omicron sublineages have dominated global SARS-CoV-2 circulation since late 2021, but there aren't enough multi-year datasets that detail lineage dynamics and genomic surveillance performance in North Africa. The National Influenza and Other Respiratory Viruses Laboratory in Tunisia has been conducting integrated SARS-CoV-2 genomic surveillance for four years. METHODS: Between 1 November 2021 and 30 September 2025, 8,635 nasopharyngeal swabs (NPS) received through the national sentinel network were tested for SARS-CoV-2 by real-time RT-PCR, of which 1,020 (11.8%) were positive. A total of 669 (65.6%) positive samples were successfully sequenced using Illumina RNA Prep with Enrichment and a respiratory virus panel. Pango lineages and GISAID clades were assigned with standard tools, and sequencing coverage, geographic representativeness, turnaround times, temporal trends, lineage diversity, mutational profiles, and phylogenetic placement were summarized descriptively. RESULTS: The overall SARS-CoV-2 positivity rate was 11.8%. Median governorate-level sequencing coverage among RT-PCR-positive samples was 60.0% (IQR 28.6-88.9), and the share of sequences closely matched the share of positives (r = 0.992), indicating near-proportional sampling.While SARS-CoV-2-positive NPS displayed several waves, including substantial peaks in mid-2022 and mid-2023 and subsequent winter peaks, each linked to the establishment or replacement of dominant Omicron lineages, testing volumes indicated recurrent winter rises. Among the 669 sequenced SARS-CoV-2-positive samples, 92 (13.8%) showed co-detection with at least one other respiratory virus, including 16 (2.4%) involving influenza viruses.XBB* lineages accounted for 25.0% of genomes, followed by BA.4/BA.5* (22.1%), JN.1* and descendants (13.6%), BA.2* (12.6%), and BA.1* (9.0%), while Delta represented 8.7% of genomes; the remaining 9.1% belonged to other lineages, including pre-Omicron variants and non-XBB recombinants. Almost all genomes belonged to Omicron-associated GISAID clades GK and GRA. Overall, sequencing quality was high (mapped reads typically ≥0.9), while Tunisian SARS-CoV-2 genomes showed a progressive increase in amino acid changes-from ~30-50 substitutions in early Delta/BA.1/BA.2 to >70-80 in later XBB and JN.1* sublineages, with some recombinants approaching 100 substitutions. Phylogenetic analyses showed that Tunisian genomes clustered within globally circulating Delta and Omicron clades. CONCLUSIONS: Rapid Omicron sublineage turnover and co-detections with other respiratory viruses, including influenza, were captured by genomic monitoring integrated into Tunisia's influenza-based sentinel network, which achieved broad sequencing coverage and overall near-proportional sampling despite subnational heterogeneity.This integrated, multi-pathogen approach provides a scalable model for sustained genomic surveillance and future respiratory pandemic preparedness in the region.
papers.abstract_zh: 背景:自2021年底以来,奥密克戎亚谱系在全球严重急性呼吸综合征冠状病毒2传播中占据主导地位,但缺乏详细描述谱系动态和严重急性呼吸综合征冠状病毒2表现的多年度数据集,特别是在北非地区。突尼斯的国家流感及其他呼吸道病毒实验室已连续四年进行整合的严重急性呼吸综合征冠状病毒2监测。方法:2021年11月1日至2025年9月30日期间,通过国家哨点网络收集了8,635份鼻咽拭子(NPS),其中1,020份(11.8%)通过实时RT-PCR检测为严重急性呼吸综合征冠状病毒2阳性。在这些阳性样本中,669份(65.6%)使用Illumina RNA Prep与富集和呼吸道病毒面板成功进行了测序。使用标准工具分配了Pango谱系和GISAID分支,并对测序覆盖率、地理代表性、周转时间、时间趋势、谱系多样性、突变特征和系统发育位置进行了描述性总结。结果:总体严重急性呼吸综合征冠状病毒2阳性率是11.8%。在RT-PCR阳性样本中,省市级测序覆盖率的中位数为60.0%(IQR 28.6-88.9),且序列比例与阳性比例高度相关(r = 0.992),表明采样接近比例。尽管严重急性呼吸综合征冠状病毒2阳性鼻咽拭子显示出多个波峰,包括2022年中期和2023年中期的显著高峰以及随后的冬季高峰,每个高峰都与主导奥密克戎谱系的确立或取代有关,但检测量显示冬季有反复上升的趋势。在669份测序的严重急性呼吸综合征冠状病毒2阳性样本中,92份(13.8%)与其他呼吸道病毒共检,其中16份(2.4%)涉及流感病毒。XBB*谱系占严重急性呼吸综合征冠状病毒2的25.0%,其次是BA.4/BA.5*(22.1%)、JN.1*及其后代(13.6%)、BA.2*(12.6%)和BA.1*(9.0%),而Delta占严重急性呼吸综合征冠状病毒2的8.7%;其余9.1%属于其他谱系,包括奥密克戎前变异株和非XBB重组株。几乎所有严重急性呼吸综合征冠状病毒2都属于与奥密克戎相关的GISAID分支GK和GRA。总体而言,测序质量较高(通常映射读数≥0.9),而突尼斯的严重急性呼吸综合征冠状病毒2在后期XBB和JN.1*亚谱系中显示出氨基酸变化的逐步增加,从早期Delta/BA.1/BA.2的约30-50个替换增加到后期的>70-80个替换,某些重组株甚至接近100个替换。系统发育分析显示,突尼斯的严重急性呼吸综合征冠状病毒2样本在Delta和奥密克戎全球传播的分支内聚类。结论:通过将基因组监测整合到突尼斯基于流感的哨点网络中,该研究捕捉到了奥密克戎亚谱系的快速更替以及与其他呼吸道病毒(包括流感病毒)的共检现象。尽管存在次国家层面的异质性,该方法仍实现了广泛的测序覆盖率和总体接近比例的采样,为该地区持续的严重急性呼吸综合征冠状病毒2监测和未来呼吸道大流行准备提供了一个可扩展的模型。科学与公共卫生意义:这些发现为突尼斯及类似地区严重急性呼吸综合征冠状病毒2的监测、预防和控制策略提供了信息,强调了整合多病原体方法在严重急性呼吸综合征冠状病毒2监测和大流行准备中的重要性。局限性与证据强度:该研究的局限性包括由于次国家层面的异质性可能导致的采样偏差,以及依赖哨点网络可能无法覆盖所有病例。由于这些局限性,证据强度中等。

papers.title: Separating the effects of immune waning and viral evolution on COVID-19 vaccine effectiveness reveals improved effectiveness of updated vaccines
papers.abstract: Abstract The continued evolution of SARS-CoV-2 has led to regular updates of the COVID-19 vaccine immunogen. However, the exact benefits of these updates for vaccine effectiveness in a real world context are difficult to evaluate. We performed a comprehensive meta-analysis of booster vaccine effectiveness in studies identified through the ViewHub systematic review. We integrated evidence from 44 studies reporting on effectiveness of mRNA booster vaccines containing XBB.1.5, JN.1 and KP.2 immunogens to assess the combined impact of booster immunogen, time since vaccination and calendar time at which a study was conducted. We estimate that the relative risk of severe disease increases by 9% [95%CI 7.4-10.5] each month following booster administration, likely due to antibody waning, and by an additional 2.4% [95%CI 1.2-3.6] for each calendar month, likely due to antigenic drift. Our findings show that COVID-19 booster vaccine effectiveness declines both with time after vaccination as well as calendar time since the vaccine immunogen emerged. This reinforces the need for regularly and timely vaccine immunogen updates.

papers.title_zh: Separating the effects of immune waning and viral evolution on COVID-19 vaccine effectiveness reveals improved effectiveness of updated vaccines
papers.source_body_en: Abstract The continued evolution of SARS-CoV-2 has led to regular updates of the COVID-19 vaccine immunogen. However, the exact benefits of these updates for vaccine effectiveness in a real world context are difficult to evaluate. We performed a comprehensive meta-analysis of booster vaccine effectiveness in studies identified through the ViewHub systematic review. We integrated evidence from 44 studies reporting on effectiveness of mRNA booster vaccines containing XBB.1.5, JN.1 and KP.2 immunogens to assess the combined impact of booster immunogen, time since vaccination and calendar time at which a study was conducted. We estimate that the relative risk of severe disease increases by 9% [95%CI 7.4-10.5] each month following booster administration, likely due to antibody waning, and by an additional 2.4% [95%CI 1.2-3.6] for each calendar month, likely due to antigenic drift. Our findings show that COVID-19 booster vaccine effectiveness declines both with time after vaccination as well as calendar time since the vaccine immunogen emerged. This reinforces the need for regularly and timely vaccine immunogen updates.

papers.title: Association of SARS-CoV-2 Positivity in Travelers and Community Prevalence: Serial Cross-Sectional Data From the Traveler-based Genomic Surveillance Program
papers.abstract: Objectives: As SARS-CoV-2 testing has declined, estimating disease prevalence has become challenging. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention’s Traveler-based Genomic Surveillance (TGS) program collects voluntary samples from arriving international travelers to detect SARS-CoV-2 variants. We assessed the correlation between SARS-CoV-2 positivity in travelers and community case data for their corresponding countries of origin. Methods: From December 6, 2021, through January 22, 2023, travelers (aged ≥18 y) arriving at selected US airports provided self-collected nasal swabs, which were pooled by country of origin and tested for SARS-CoV-2 using reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction. We compared weekly SARS-CoV-2 positivity rates from travelers who arrived from 6 countries (Brazil, France, Germany, India, South Africa, United Kingdom) with weekly community case rates for that same country. For the United Kingdom, we also compared traveler data with data from the UK Coronavirus (COVID-19) Infection Survey. We conducted correlation analyses by country and divided data into intervals to control for time-varying confounders. Using Spearman rank correlation, we assessed the correlations between traveler data and community or household data. Results: SARS-CoV-2 positivity in travelers and community case data frequently demonstrated concordance (66.7% of time intervals were significantly correlated, defined as P < .05). After June 12, 2022, when predeparture SARS-CoV-2 testing was no longer required of US-bound travelers, sample positivity among travelers arriving from the United Kingdom was significantly correlated with positivity estimates from the UK COVID-19 Infection Survey ( r s = 0.76; P < .001). Conclusions: Data from travelers may reflect trends similar to country-level SARS-CoV-2 transmission. When community testing is limited, public health authorities could consider using TGS or similar systems to monitor transmission activity.

papers.source_body_en: Objectives: As SARS-CoV-2 testing has declined, estimating disease prevalence has become challenging. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention’s Traveler-based Genomic Surveillance (TGS) program collects voluntary samples from arriving international travelers to detect SARS-CoV-2 variants. We assessed the correlation between SARS-CoV-2 positivity in travelers and community case data for their corresponding countries of origin. Methods: From December 6, 2021, through January 22, 2023, travelers (aged ≥18 y) arriving at selected US airports provided self-collected nasal swabs, which were pooled by country of origin and tested for SARS-CoV-2 using reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction. We compared weekly SARS-CoV-2 positivity rates from travelers who arrived from 6 countries (Brazil, France, Germany, India, South Africa, United Kingdom) with weekly community case rates for that same country. For the United Kingdom, we also compared traveler data with data from the UK Coronavirus (COVID-19) Infection Survey. We conducted correlation analyses by country and divided data into intervals to control for time-varying confounders. Using Spearman rank correlation, we assessed the correlations between traveler data and community or household data. Results: SARS-CoV-2 positivity in travelers and community case data frequently demonstrated concordance (66.7% of time intervals were significantly correlated, defined as P < .05). After June 12, 2022, when predeparture SARS-CoV-2 testing was no longer required of US-bound travelers, sample positivity among travelers arriving from the United Kingdom was significantly correlated with positivity estimates from the UK COVID-19 Infection Survey ( r s = 0.76; P < .001). Conclusions: Data from travelers may reflect trends similar to country-level SARS-CoV-2 transmission. When community testing is limited, public health authorities could consider using TGS or similar systems to monitor transmission activity.

analysis_zh.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: 当社区检测受限时,公共卫生部门可以考虑使用TGS或类似系统来监测传播活动。

papers.title: Complementary Roles of RT-PCR and Next-Generation Sequencing in Post-Vaccination SARS-CoV-2 Infection: Clinical Diagnosis, Genomic Characterization, and Surveillance
papers.abstract: SARS-CoV-2 infection after vaccination remains a clinical and public-health challenge because protection against infection may vary with time since vaccination, host factors, previous infection, and ongoing viral evolution. Although vaccination substantially reduces the risk of severe COVID-19, post-vaccination infections may still occur and may be mild, atypical, or asymptomatic. This narrative review examines the complementary roles of reverse-transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) and next-generation sequencing (NGS) in the diagnosis, genomic characterization, and surveillance of post-vaccination SARS-CoV-2 infection. RT-PCR remains the first-line method for confirming acute infection because it is rapid, widely available, and clinically actionable, although its clinical performance depends on appropriate specimen collection and timing. NGS complements RT-PCR by providing viral genomic characterization, including lineage assignment, mutation detection, investigation of suspected transmission clusters, and population-level surveillance. Sequencing may provide additional value in selected settings, particularly suspected reinfection, persistent infection in selected immunocompromised patients, outbreak investigations, and representative or event-triggered genomic surveillance. Its use should therefore be guided by a predefined clinical, epidemiological, or surveillance objective rather than applied routinely to all post-vaccination infections. An integrated strategy combining first-line RT-PCR with objective-driven sequencing can preserve diagnostic efficiency while providing genomic information when it is most likely to influence patient-level investigation, infection-control assessment, or public-health surveillance.

Sequencing may provide additional value in selected settings, particularly suspected reinfection, persistent infection in selected immunocompromised patients, outbreak investigations, and representative or event-triggered genomic surveillance. Its use should therefore be guided by a predefined clinical, epidemiological, or surveillance objective rather than applied routinely to all post-vaccination infections. An integrated strategy combining first-line RT-PCR with objective-driven sequencing can preserve diagnostic efficiency while providing genomic information when it is most likely to influence patient-level investigation, infection-control assessment, or public-health surveillance.

papers.title: COVID-19 vaccine effectiveness in people on immunosuppressive therapies: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: People on immunosuppressive therapies are at increased risk of severe COVID-19, yet vaccine efficacy in these individuals has been inadequately assessed in randomised controlled trials. This systematic review and meta-analysis aims to examine vaccine effectiveness in people with medical conditions commonly treated with conventional synthetic or targeted immunosuppressive therapies. METHODS: We searched PubMed and Scopus from database inception and Embase from Jan 1, 2020, until Dec 5, 2025. We included randomised controlled trials, cohort studies, and case-control studies of COVID-19 vaccines in adults with haematological malignancies or autoimmune and immune-mediated inflammatory disorders. Studies were eligible if they were published in English and reported vaccine effectiveness or a relative risk (RR) measure for preventing SARS-CoV-2 infection, hospitalisation, severe disease, or death. We excluded studies of organ transplant recipients and patients with other conditions (eg, HIV or non-haematologic cancers). Data were extracted by one author (SRK or ES) and verified by another author (SRK, KME, ES, CP, PH, RVH, RVJ, or SCS). Risk of bias was assessed independently by two authors (KME and EE) using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale. Effect measures were pooled using random-effects meta-analysis with inverse variance weighting. I2 with 95% CIs were reported as measures of between-study heterogeneity. This review was registered with PROSPERO (CRD42023434975). FINDINGS: Our database search identified 3316 studies, and one additional study was identified from citation searching. 35 studies were eligible for inclusion in the review, of which 34 were included in the meta-analysis (one study was excluded due to no cases in all arms). Of the 34 included studies, 17 reported vaccine effectiveness against COVID-19 outcomes in people on immunosuppressive therapies compared with unvaccinated individuals, 16 reported RR measures in vaccinated individuals on immunosuppressive therapies compared with vaccinated healthy controls, and one reported both. Of the 34 included studies, risk of bias was rated as good in 21 (62%) studies, as fair in four (12%), and as poor in nine (26%). Clinical outcomes reported across the studies were: infection in 28 (82%), hospitalisation or severe disease in 16 (47%), and death in eight (24%). Vaccine effectiveness was 82·3% (95% CI 72·4-88·7, I2=96·8%) against SARS-CoV-2 infection with pre-omicron variants after three vaccinations and 88·4% (82·8-92·3, 73·9%) against hospitalisation. Among vaccinated individuals on immunosuppressive therapies, the RR compared with that in vaccinated healthy individuals was 1·57 (1·25-1·96, I2=89·7%) for SARS-CoV-2 infection, 3·72 (1·63-8·47, 85·5%) for hospitalisation, and 3·14 (1·51-6·54, 75·2%) for death. INTERPRETATION: This analysis shows a substantial benefit of vaccination for people on immunosuppressive therapy, particularly after three vaccine doses and against severe outcomes. It also highlights a significantly higher risk of hospitalisation and death in this group than in vaccinated healthy individuals. Assessing booster vaccine effectiveness in these populations against current circulating variants and with updated vaccines remains a priority. FUNDING: National Health and Medical Research Council (Australia).

analysis.summary_en: This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to assess the effectiveness of COVID-19 vaccines in individuals on immunosuppressive therapies, a population at higher risk for severe disease. The study included randomised controlled trials, cohort studies, and case-control studies of vaccines in adults with haematological malignancies or autoimmune and immune-mediated inflammatory disorders. A comprehensive search of PubMed, Scopus, and Embase was conducted, and 35 studies were eligible for inclusion, with 34 included in the meta-analysis. The results showed vaccine effectiveness of 82·3% (95% CI 72·4-88·7) against SARS-CoV-2 infection with pre-omicron variants after three vaccinations and 88·4% (82·8-92·3) against hospitalisation. Among vaccinated individuals on immunosuppressive therapies, the relative risk compared with vaccinated healthy individuals was 1·57 (1·25-1·96) for infection, 3·72 (1·63-8·47) for hospitalisation, and 3·14 (1·51-6·54) for death. The authors interpreted these findings as demonstrating a substantial benefit of vaccination for people on immunosuppressive therapy, particularly against severe outcomes, while also highlighting a significantly higher risk of hospitalisation and death in this group compared to vaccinated healthy individuals. The study's evidence strength is moderate due to the heterogeneity of the included studies and the potential for bias.

papers.title_zh: COVID-19 vaccine effectiveness in people on immunosuppressive therapies: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
papers.source_body_en: BACKGROUND: People on immunosuppressive therapies are at increased risk of severe COVID-19, yet vaccine efficacy in these individuals has been inadequately assessed in randomised controlled trials. This systematic review and meta-analysis aims to examine vaccine effectiveness in people with medical conditions commonly treated with conventional synthetic or targeted immunosuppressive therapies. METHODS: We searched PubMed and Scopus from database inception and Embase from Jan 1, 2020, until Dec 5, 2025. We included randomised controlled trials, cohort studies, and case-control studies of COVID-19 vaccines in adults with haematological malignancies or autoimmune and immune-mediated inflammatory disorders. Studies were eligible if they were published in English and reported vaccine effectiveness or a relative risk (RR) measure for preventing SARS-CoV-2 infection, hospitalisation, severe disease, or death. We excluded studies of organ transplant recipients and patients with other conditions (eg, HIV or non-haematologic cancers). Data were extracted by one author (SRK or ES) and verified by another author (SRK, KME, ES, CP, PH, RVH, RVJ, or SCS). Risk of bias was assessed independently by two authors (KME and EE) using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale. Effect measures were pooled using random-effects meta-analysis with inverse variance weighting. I2 with 95% CIs were reported as measures of between-study heterogeneity. This review was registered with PROSPERO (CRD42023434975). FINDINGS: Our database search identified 3316 studies, and one additional study was identified from citation searching. 35 studies were eligible for inclusion in the review, of which 34 were included in the meta-analysis (one study was excluded due to no cases in all arms). Of the 34 included studies, 17 reported vaccine effectiveness against COVID-19 outcomes in people on immunosuppressive therapies compared with unvaccinated individuals, 16 reported RR measures in vaccinated individuals on immunosuppressive therapies compared with vaccinated healthy controls, and one reported both. Of the 34 included studies, risk of bias was rated as good in 21 (62%) studies, as fair in four (12%), and as poor in nine (26%). Clinical outcomes reported across the studies were: infection in 28 (82%), hospitalisation or severe disease in 16 (47%), and death in eight (24%). Vaccine effectiveness was 82·3% (95% CI 72·4-88·7, I2=96·8%) against SARS-CoV-2 infection with pre-omicron variants after three vaccinations and 88·4% (82·8-92·3, 73·9%) against hospitalisation. Among vaccinated individuals on immunosuppressive therapies, the RR compared with that in vaccinated healthy individuals was 1·57 (1·25-1·96, I2=89·7%) for SARS-CoV-2 infection, 3·72 (1·63-8·47, 85·5%) for hospitalisation, and 3·14 (1·51-6·54, 75·2%) for death. INTERPRETATION: This analysis shows a substantial benefit of vaccination for people on immunosuppressive therapy, particularly after three vaccine doses and against severe outcomes. It also highlights a significantly higher risk of hospitalisation and death in this group than in vaccinated healthy individuals. Assessing booster vaccine effectiveness in these populations against current circulating variants and with updated vaccines remains a priority. FUNDING: National Health and Medical Research Council (Australia).

papers.title: COVID-19 mortality risk among people with HIV in Florida before and after the introduction of COVID-19 vaccines: A population-based study
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVE: Assess associations between COVID-19 vaccine availability and differences in COVID-19 mortality risk across subgroups among 122,527 people with HIV (PWH) in Florida. METHODS: Analyzed HIV surveillance data, Social Vulnerability Index (SVI), and Rural-Urban Commuting Area Codes using a competing risks model to compare COVID-19 mortality among PWH before (3/1/2020-4/30/2021) and during (5/1/2021-12/31/2021) vaccine availability. RESULTS: Overall COVID-19 mortality rates increased from before to during the vaccine availability period (22.3 vs. 27.5 per 100,000 person-months), driven in part by the Delta variant surge in mid-to-late 2021. Compared to Non-Hispanic White (NHW) PWH, adjusted COVID-19 mortality hazards remained elevated for Non-Hispanic Black (NHB) PWH both before (HR 2.06, 95% CI 1.45-2.91) and during (HR 1.60, 95% CI 1.13-2.27) vaccine availability. For Hispanic PWH, the relative hazard compared to NHW was elevated before (HR 2.24, 95% CI 1.55-3.23) and attenuated during vaccine availability (HR 1.03, 95% CI 0.68-1.57). In the final model, living in ZIP Code-level areas of high social vulnerability (overall SVI high vs. low) was associated with elevated hazard during vaccine availability (HR 1.75, 95% CI 1.04-2.97). CONCLUSIONS: Overall COVID-19 mortality rates were higher during the vaccine availability period (27.5 vs. 22.3 per 100,000 person-months); however, subgroup patterns varied substantially. Inequities persisted in key subgroups and were most pronounced among PWH living in more socially vulnerable areas. These observational comparisons do not estimate the causal effect of vaccination uptake. PUBLIC HEALTH IMPLICATIONS: Tailored vaccination strategies and structural interventions remain essential to advancing equity in pandemic response among PWH.

papers.title_original: COVID-19 mortality risk among people with HIV in Florida before and after the introduction of COVID-19 vaccines: A population-based study

analysis.research_question_and_background: This study aimed to assess associations between the availability of COVID-19 vaccines and differences in mortality risk among people with HIV (PWH) in Florida, addressing the need to understand how vaccine access might influence outcomes in this subgroup during the pandemic.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study analyzed HIV surveillance data, Social Vulnerability Index (SVI), and Rural-Urban Commuting Area Codes from 122,527 people with HIV in Florida, comparing mortality rates before and during the vaccine availability period (March 1, 2020–April 30, 2021 and May 1, 2021–December 31, 2021, respectively).
analysis.methods: A competing risks model was used to compare mortality rates among people with HIV before and during the vaccine availability period, incorporating data from HIV surveillance, SVI, and Rural-Urban Commuting Area Codes.
analysis.main_results: Overall COVID-19 mortality rates increased from 22.3 to 27.5 per 100,000 person-months during the vaccine availability period, driven by the Delta variant surge. Adjusted mortality hazards remained elevated for Non-Hispanic Black PWH both before and during vaccine availability, with HRs of 2.06 (95% CI 1.45-2.91) and 1.60 (95% CI 1.13-2.27), respectively. For Hispanic PWH, the relative hazard compared to Non-Hispanic White PWH was elevated before vaccine availability (HR 2.24, 95% CI 1.55-3.23) but attenuated during (HR 1.03, 95% CI 0.68-1.57). Living in ZIP Code-level areas of high social vulnerability was associated with elevated hazard during vaccine availability (HR 1.75, 95% CI 1.04-2.97).
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted that subgroup patterns of mortality varied substantially, with inequities persisting among key subgroups, particularly those in socially vulnerable areas, highlighting the need for targeted interventions.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings inform the importance of tailored vaccination strategies and structural interventions to address disparities in mortality risk among people with HIV during the pandemic, particularly in socially vulnerable communities.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is observational and does not estimate the causal effect of vaccination uptake, which limits the strength of the evidence. However, the use of a competing risks model and comprehensive data sources provides a moderate level of confidence in the findings.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigated the impact of COVID-19 vaccine availability on mortality risk among people with HIV in Florida, comparing outcomes before and during the vaccine rollout period. It found that overall mortality rates increased during the vaccine availability period, driven by the Delta variant surge. Mortality hazards remained elevated for Non-Hispanic Black PWH both before and during vaccine availability, while Hispanic PWH showed a reduction in relative hazard during the period. Social vulnerability was also linked to higher mortality risk. The study highlights persistent inequities and underscores the need for targeted strategies to improve outcomes among vulnerable subgroups. However, the observational nature of the study limits causal inference.

papers.title: Maternal mortality in pregnant women with COVID-19 during the early pandemic period (2019–2022): a systematic review of published cases
papers.abstract: Pregnant women were at higher risk for Coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19), and this infection can lead to adverse effects such as maternal mortality, preterm delivery, and miscarriage. However, there has been limited information available about COVID-19 in pregnancy. This study aimed to report maternal mortality in pregnant women with COVID-19 and how COVID-19 is related to their death, clinical features, and laboratory changes. We conducted a systematic search on PubMed/Medline, Web of Science, and Embase to identify studies addressing maternal mortality and COVID-19 in pregnancy during 2019–2022. The following terms were used: [“maternal mortality”] AND [“COVID-19” OR “SARS-CoV-2” OR “2019-nCoV”]. Fourteen relevant research articles were included in our study. The highest maternal mortality rate due to COVID-19 was reported in the third trimester and postpartum, with 133 mothers (133/172). The most common comorbidities included cardiovascular disease (20%), diabetes (18.3%), and obesity (12.5%). Cardiopulmonary complications caused by SARS-CoV-2 were identified as leading cause of maternal death. Based on the results of the current study, it is evident that COVID-19 and its complications played a significant role in maternal mortality in pregnant women during the early pandemic period (2019–2022). Importantly, these findings reflect an era before widespread vaccination and population immunity. Since 2022, the emergence of new variants (e.g., Omicron) and high vaccination coverage have substantially altered COVID-19 severity in pregnancy. Therefore, these results should be interpreted as historical baseline data rather than current risk estimates. Further studies examining maternal outcomes in the post-vaccination era are strongly recommended.

papers.title: ACE2 dysregulation and lipid metabolism: Mechanistic interplay between COVID-19 and neurodegeneration
papers.abstract: Angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (ACE2) is the primary cellular receptor of SARS-CoV-2. It is a key regulator of the renin-angiotensin system (RAS) and modulates blood pressure and inflammatory pathways. ACE2 converts pro-inflammatory angiotensin II into the vasoprotective peptide, angiotensin (1-7). This is strongly influenced by the lipid composition of the plasma membrane. Cholesterol-rich lipid rafts play an important role in determining receptor localisation and viral accessibility. Dyslipidaemia, which is common in obesity, diabetes, and metabolic syndrome, has been associated with an increased susceptibility to severe COVID-19 and may amplify systemic inflammation. Aberrant lipid metabolism also contributes to neurodegenerative disorders, including Alzheimer's and Parkinson's diseases, which drive neuroinflammation, synaptic dysfunction, and blood-brain barrier impairment. Notably, similar disturbances and systemic inflammation are increasingly recognised in patients with Long COVID, suggesting overlapping mechanisms that may exacerbate or accelerate neurodegenerative processes. This review explores the interplay between ACE2 regulation, lipid metabolism, and systemic inflammation in COVID-19, with a particular focus on their implications for neurological health. Uniquely, we highlighted the intersection of ACE2 and lipid-related alterations in patients with Long COVID and their potential contribution to the progression of neurodegenerative diseases. In addition, we reviewed therapeutic strategies targeting ACE2, including recombinant soluble ACE2, ACE2-based nanotherapeutics, and lipid-focused interventions, aimed at mitigating acute infection, systemic inflammation, and persistent neurological sequelae. Understanding these mechanisms is essential to prevent long-term neurological consequences of the COVID-19 pandemic.

analysis.scope_and_question: The review focuses on SARS-CoV-2, specifically examining the interplay between ACE2 regulation, lipid metabolism, and systemic inflammation in the context of COVID-19 and its neurological implications. It addresses the role of ACE2 as the primary receptor for SARS-CoV-2 and its involvement in modulating inflammatory pathways and blood pressure. The central question is how these mechanisms contribute to the progression of neurodegenerative diseases, particularly in patients with Long COVID.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: The review is a narrative synthesis of existing literature, with no explicit mention of systematic search methods, databases, or meta-analysis. It includes general background information on ACE2 and lipid metabolism, as well as results from studies linking dyslipidaemia to severe COVID-19 and Long COVID. The review does not report on study counts or eligibility criteria.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: The review concludes that ACE2 dysregulation and lipid metabolism alterations are interconnected and play a significant role in the pathophysiology of severe COVID-19 and Long COVID. It highlights that these factors may contribute to neuroinflammation, synaptic dysfunction, and blood-brain barrier impairment, potentially exacerbating or accelerating neurodegenerative processes. The review also notes that understanding these mechanisms is essential for preventing long-term neurological consequences of the pandemic.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: The review identifies a lack of comprehensive studies on the specific mechanisms linking ACE2 and lipid metabolism to neurodegenerative diseases. It also notes that while dyslipidaemia is associated with increased susceptibility to severe COVID-19, the exact causal relationship and its impact on neurological outcomes remain unclear. Additionally, the review acknowledges that the role of lipid rafts in ACE2 localization and viral entry is not fully understood.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: The review suggests that future research should focus on elucidating the molecular mechanisms by which ACE2 and lipid metabolism interact in the context of SARS-CoV-2 infection and Long COVID. It also recommends exploring therapeutic strategies targeting ACE2 and lipid metabolism to mitigate acute infection, systemic inflammation, and persistent neurological sequelae. Furthermore, it highlights the need for improved surveillance and diagnostic tools to identify patients at risk for these complications.

analysis.summary_en: This review explores the interplay between ACE2 regulation, lipid metabolism, and systemic inflammation in SARS-CoV-2 infection and its neurological consequences. It highlights that ACE2, the primary receptor for SARS-CoV-2, modulates inflammatory pathways and blood pressure, and its function is influenced by the lipid composition of the plasma membrane. Dyslipidaemia, common in metabolic disorders, is linked to increased susceptibility to severe COVID-19 and Long COVID, which may contribute to neuroinflammation and neurodegenerative processes. The review underscores the importance of understanding these mechanisms to develop targeted interventions and prevent long-term neurological effects of the pandemic.

Dyslipidaemia, which is common in obesity, diabetes, and metabolic syndrome, has been associated with an increased susceptibility to severe COVID-19 and may amplify systemic inflammation. Aberrant lipid metabolism also contributes to neurodegenerative disorders, including Alzheimer's and Parkinson's diseases, which drive neuroinflammation, synaptic dysfunction, and blood-brain barrier impairment. Notably, similar disturbances and systemic inflammation are increasingly recognised in patients with Long COVID, suggesting overlapping mechanisms that may exacerbate or accelerate neurodegenerative processes. This review explores the interplay between ACE2 regulation, lipid metabolism, and systemic inflammation in COVID-19, with a particular focus on their implications for neurological health. Uniquely, we highlighted the intersection of ACE2 and lipid-related alterations in patients with Long COVID and their potential contribution to the progression of neurodegenerative diseases. In addition, we reviewed therapeutic strategies targeting ACE2, including recombinant soluble ACE2, ACE2-based nanotherapeutics, and lipid-focused interventions, aimed at mitigating acute infection, systemic inflammation, and persistent neurological sequelae. Understanding these mechanisms is essential to prevent long-term neurological consequences of the COVID-19 pandemic.

papers.title: Nanotechnology-Enabled Therapeutics for Global Viral Diseases: From COVID-19 to Emerging Viral Infections
papers.abstract: The threat of viral disease remains one of the biggest concerns regarding global public health, as is evident from the recent global pandemic caused by the coronavirus and the repeated outbreaks of new pathogens like influenza virus, Ebola virus, Zika virus, Nipah virus, monkey pox virus, and coronaviruses that are pathogenic. Traditional approaches to antiviral therapy may pose certain limitations, like poor bioavailability, systemic toxicity, mutation rate of the virus, multiple drug resistance, and the inability of drugs to target tissues specifically. The development of nanotechnology has been a breakthrough solution in overcoming the limitations posed by traditional methods. This review aims at assessing the latest advancements in the field of nanotechnology in terms of developing therapeutic interventions in viral diseases, especially COVID-19 and other emerging viral infections. These approaches improve drug stability, bioavailability, controlled drug delivery, and immunogenicity, all while minimizing toxicity in the body. Despite the fact that there are several promising applications for nanomedicines in both pre-clinical and clinical studies, issues pertaining to biosafety, scalability, and regulation prevent their full clinical implementation. Nanotechnology-based treatments constitute a paradigm shift within antiviral medicine with respect to their integration of targeted drug delivery, immune manipulation, and precision medicine. It is important that further interdisciplinary efforts, regulation, and clinical trials contribute to the development of such nanotechnologies to combat viral pandemics in the present and in the future. Keywords: Nanotechnology; Viral infections; COVID-19; Antiviral drug delivery; Nanovaccines.
papers.journal: Journal of Drug Delivery and Therapeutics

papers.title_zh: Nanotechnology-Enabled Therapeutics for Global Viral Diseases: From COVID-19 to Emerging Viral Infections
papers.source_body_en: The threat of viral disease remains one of the biggest concerns regarding global public health, as is evident from the recent global pandemic caused by the coronavirus and the repeated outbreaks of new pathogens like influenza virus, Ebola virus, Zika virus, Nipah virus, monkey pox virus, and coronaviruses that are pathogenic. Traditional approaches to antiviral therapy may pose certain limitations, like poor bioavailability, systemic toxicity, mutation rate of the virus, multiple drug resistance, and the inability of drugs to target tissues specifically. The development of nanotechnology has been a breakthrough solution in overcoming the limitations posed by traditional methods. This review aims at assessing the latest advancements in the field of nanotechnology in terms of developing therapeutic interventions in viral diseases, especially COVID-19 and other emerging viral infections. These approaches improve drug stability, bioavailability, controlled drug delivery, and immunogenicity, all while minimizing toxicity in the body. Despite the fact that there are several promising applications for nanomedicines in both pre-clinical and clinical studies, issues pertaining to biosafety, scalability, and regulation prevent their full clinical implementation. Nanotechnology-based treatments constitute a paradigm shift within antiviral medicine with respect to their integration of targeted drug delivery, immune manipulation, and precision medicine. It is important that further interdisciplinary efforts, regulation, and clinical trials contribute to the development of such nanotechnologies to combat viral pandemics in the present and in the future. Keywords: Nanotechnology; Viral infections; COVID-19; Antiviral drug delivery; Nanovaccines.

papers.title: SARS-CoV-2 and RSV external quality assessment on molecular detection and variant typing in European expert laboratories in 2025
papers.abstract: We herein report on the fourth SARS-CoV-2 wet-lab external quality assessment (EQA) and the second organized by the AURORAE consortium to assess the diagnostic capabilities of European expert public health laboratories. Diagnostic capabilities were investigated regarding SARS-CoV-2 and, for the first time, respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) groups A and B. A 10-sample panel containing various SARS-CoV-2 variants, RSV lineages, a common cold coronavirus, and a negative control was produced and validated. Participants were invited by the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) and asked to submit results and assay details via electronic forms. Thirty-seven laboratories from 32 European countries participated. All panel samples were identified correctly via molecular detection by 23 participating laboratories (23/37; 62%). Commercial assays were used most often (23/37; 62%), in comparison to in-house assays (14/37; 38%), or a combination of both (8/37; 22%). RSV groups were correctly determined by 20 laboratories (20/37; 54%). The optional task of SARS-CoV-2 variant typing was performed by 20 laboratories using next-generation sequencing. Thirteen laboratories successfully generated SARS-CoV-2 sequences. Six laboratories performed optional RSV sequencing, with only two obtaining sequences. The current and previous EQAs show that molecular detection of SARS-CoV-2 within Europe has improved over time and is now at a consistently high level. Molecular detection of RSV samples with low viral load was challenging, as was lineage identification for low-concentration specimens. Routine monitoring of diagnostic and surveillance assays via EQAs remains key to maintaining rapid and long-lasting public health laboratory response systems.IMPORTANCEExternal quality assessments (EQAs) are essential for ensuring reliable and consistent diagnostic testing. They provide an objective way to evaluate laboratory performance, identify weaknesses, and drive improvements, as well as ensuring compliance with accreditation standards. Furthermore, participating in EQAs strengthens the contributions to public health disease surveillance and threat detection on national and transborder scales. During the SARS-CoV-2 pandemic, EQAs were vital for maintaining accuracy in the setting of increasing testing demands and emerging variants. Broadening of diagnostic testing to a wider panel of viruses, including respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), requires continuous performance monitoring to ensure accuracy and reliability. Ongoing development of vaccines and therapeutics, which may drive the emergence of new mutations, further underscores the need for regular evaluation of test effectiveness. By standardizing methods and reducing errors, EQAs ensure trustworthy and comparable results across laboratories. Regular participation in EQAs strengthens molecular diagnostics and variant surveillance.

papers.abstract_original: We herein report on the fourth SARS-CoV-2 wet-lab external quality assessment (EQA) and the second organized by the AURORAE consortium to assess the diagnostic capabilities of European expert public health laboratories. Diagnostic capabilities were investigated regarding SARS-CoV-2 and, for the first time, respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) groups A and B. A 10-sample panel containing various SARS-CoV-2 variants, RSV lineages, a common cold coronavirus, and a negative control was produced and validated. Participants were invited by the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) and asked to submit results and assay details via electronic forms. Thirty-seven laboratories from 32 European countries participated. All panel samples were identified correctly via molecular detection by 23 participating laboratories (23/37; 62%). Commercial assays were used most often (23/37; 62%), in comparison to in-house assays (14/37; 38%), or a combination of both (8/37; 22%). RSV groups were correctly determined by 20 laboratories (20/37; 54%). The optional task of SARS-CoV-2 variant typing was performed by 20 laboratories using next-generation sequencing. Thirteen laboratories successfully generated SARS-CoV-2 sequences. Six laboratories performed optional RSV sequencing, with only two obtaining sequences. The current and previous EQAs show that molecular detection of SARS-CoV-2 within Europe has improved over time and is now at a consistently high level. Molecular detection of RSV samples with low viral load was challenging, as was lineage identification for low-concentration specimens. Routine monitoring of diagnostic and surveillance assays via EQAs remains key to maintaining rapid and long-lasting public health laboratory response systems.IMPORTANCEExternal quality assessments (EQAs) are essential for ensuring reliable and consistent diagnostic testing. They provide an objective way to evaluate laboratory performance, identify weaknesses, and drive improvements, as well as ensuring compliance with accreditation standards. Furthermore, participating in EQAs strengthens the contributions to public health disease surveillance and threat detection on national and transborder scales. During the SARS-CoV-2 pandemic, EQAs were vital for maintaining accuracy in the setting of increasing testing demands and emerging variants. Broadening of diagnostic testing to a wider panel of viruses, including respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), requires continuous performance monitoring to ensure accuracy and reliability. Ongoing development of vaccines and therapeutics, which may drive the emergence of new mutations, further underscores the need for regular evaluation of test effectiveness. papers.abstract_zh: 我们在此报告了第四次严重急性呼吸综合征冠状病毒2湿实验室外部质量评估(EQA)和由AURORAE联盟组织的第二次评估,以评估欧洲专家公共卫生实验室的诊断能力。本次评估不仅针对严重急性呼吸综合征冠状病毒2,还首次涉及呼吸道合胞病毒(RSV)A组和B组的诊断能力。一个包含多种严重急性呼吸综合征冠状病毒2变体、RSV谱系、普通感冒冠状病毒和阴性对照的10样本面板被生产并验证。欧洲疾病预防控制中心(ECDC)邀请了来自32个欧洲国家的37个实验室参与,并要求通过电子表格提交结果和实验细节。所有面板样本中有23个实验室(23/37;62%)通过分子检测正确识别。商业试剂盒使用最为频繁(23/37;62%),其次是内部试剂盒(14/37;38%),或两者结合使用(8/37;22%)。20个实验室(20/37;54%)正确确定了RSV组。20个实验室使用下一代测序完成了可选的严重急性呼吸综合征冠状病毒2变体分型任务,其中13个实验室成功生成了严重急性呼吸综合征冠状病毒2序列。6个实验室进行了可选的RSV测序,仅有2个实验室获得了序列。当前和上一次EQA显示,欧洲范围内严重急性呼吸综合征冠状病毒2的分子检测能力随着时间的推移有所提高,并且现在保持在一个稳定的高水平。对于低病毒载量的RSV样本的分子检测以及低浓度标本的谱系鉴定都具有挑战性。通过EQA持续监测诊断和严重急性呼吸综合征冠状病毒2检测对于维持快速和持久的公共卫生实验室响应系统至关重要。在严重急性呼吸综合征冠状病毒2大流行期间,EQA对于在不断增加的检测需求和新兴变种的背景下保持准确性至关重要。将诊断测试扩展到更广泛的病毒谱系,包括呼吸道合胞病毒(RSV),需要持续的性能监控以确保准确性和可靠性。随着疫苗和治疗的发展,这可能会导致新突变的出现,进一步强调定期评估测试效果的重要性。通过标准化方法并减少错误,EQA确保了实验室之间可信赖且可比的结果。定期参与EQA加强了分子诊断和监测的监测。

papers.title: Assessing SARS-CoV-2 immune markers in vaccinated asymptomatic adults after household exposure in Canada (AB-PROTECT): a prospective cohort study.
papers.abstract: Background Determining the early immune response against SARS-CoV-2 in individuals who are vaccinated is essential for better understanding immune memory and informing COVID-19 vaccine design and use. We aimed to evaluate antibody and T-cell immune markers against SARS-CoV-2 infection among household contacts of index patients infected with SARS-CoV-2. Methods A prospective observational cohort study was created comprising vaccinated and asymptomatic adult household contacts of outpatients who presented to the Emergency Department or COVID-19 Assessment Centre at Michael Garron Hospital with a SARS-CoV-2 infection in Toronto, ON, Canada. Eligible participants were 18 years or older and had received at least two COVID-19 vaccine doses, amended to three doses after Jan 19, 2022. At enrolment, study staff collected self-reported demographic and clinical data and blood specimens to measure SARS-CoV-2 anti-spike and anti-receptor-binding domain (RBD) IgG and IgA antibodies and conduct SARS-CoV-2 spike-pseudotyped neutralisation assays, live SARS-CoV-2 microneutralisation assays, and assessments of CD4 + and CD8 + T-cell activation and functional cytokine responses to SARS-CoV-2 proteins. Participants were followed up for 28 days with repeat testing for SARS-CoV-2 infection and serological assessments. The primary outcome was SARS-CoV-2 infection within 28 days, identified by virological testing or seroconversion. Findings Between Oct 21, 2021, and Feb 21, 2023, 484 participants were enrolled; of these, for 432 participants (median age 43 years [IQR 38-50]; 217/432 [50%] were female), sufficient follow-up information was available for final analysis. SARS-CoV-2 infection developed in 210 (49%) of 432 participants, of whom 182 (87%) developed symptoms. No change was seen in the probability of infection between the 10th and 90th percentiles of anti-spike IgG levels (1, 95% CI -11 to 14) or anti-RBD IgG levels (1, -11 to 13). The predicted probability decreased by 3% for pseudoneutralisation capacity against ancestral SARS-CoV-2 (95% CI -1 to 14) and by 5% for live-virus microneutralisation titres (-22 to 13). T-cell responses were assessed in a convenience subset of 56 participants starting Jan 19, 2022, of whom 30 (54%) developed SARS-CoV-2 infection. Participants with infection had enhanced Th17 CD4 + T-cell activation responses to SARS-CoV-2 membrane protein stimulation early after household exposure (adjusted odds ratio [OR] 3·58, 95% CI 1·69-8·93). CD4 + and CD8 + T-cell cytokine polyfunctionality was similar between groups. Lower levels of omicron BA.1 spike-stimulated CD8 + T cells only coexpressing GM-CSF and TNF were also seen in participants with infection (adjusted OR 0·52, 95% CI 0·26-0·96). Interpretation Early after household exposure, binding and neutralising antibodies were similar in all participants, but differences in T-cell functional responses were evident in individuals who developed symptoms after SARS-CoV-2 infection. Funding COVID-19 Immunity Task Force Initiative Sero-Surveillance and Research Program grant.
